http:
  addr: "127.0.0.1:18113"
  read_timeout: 5s
  write_timeout: 0s  # 0s = none: streamed answers run longer than a fixed write deadline
  idle_timeout: 120s
  startup_timeout: 30s
  shutdown_timeout: 10s
  readiness_timeout: 15s

# Diagnostic pprof endpoints are opt-in and loopback-only. Use an SSH tunnel
# or an equivalent protected local access path when profiling a remote host.
profiling:
  enabled: false
  addr: "127.0.0.1:6063"

middleware:
  timeout: 30s
  logger:
    level: dev  # dev | prod

documents:
  mode: "upload-only"       # upload-only | mirror; mirror removes missing files under documents.paths
  paths:
    - "samples"
  ignore_patterns: []

ingest:
  max_attempts: 3
  initial_interval: 500ms
  max_interval: 10s
  multiplier: 2.0
  workers: 8
  max_file_bytes: 16777216       # 16 MiB per document upload/source file
  max_upload_bytes: 67108864    # 64 MiB per multipart request
  embed_batch_size: 64           # bound each Ollama embedding request
  max_chunks_per_file: 10000     # reject pathological documents before indexing

qdrant:
  addr: "localhost:17444"
  collection: "p1_subject_documents_20261003"
  top_k: 5
  prefetch_mul: 5  # store-level candidate multiplier for hybrid search legs

embedder:
  provider: "ollama"
  model: "embeddinggemma-300m-q8:latest"
  ollama_addr: "http://localhost:11434"
  dimensions: 768
  request_timeout: 60s
  query_prefix: "task: search result | query: "   # prepended to queries at search time (EmbeddingGemma task instruction; empty = off)
  # num_gpu: 0               # optional: keep embeddings on CPU when a larger answer model occupies the GPU; omitted = Ollama placement
  document_prefix: "title: none | text: "          # prepended to chunks at ingest time; requires reindex when changed
  max_input_chars: 8000                            # rune-clamp on dense embed inputs so Ollama never truncates silently (0 = off)

chunker:
  provider: "recursive"  # recursive | sentence-window (measured 2026-09-27, ADR 0033: recursive stays)
  chunk_size: 512
  chunk_overlap: 64
  window_size: 3          # sentences before+after each sentence (sentence-window only)

search:
  max_query_chars: 8192
  max_fragments: 16
  max_concurrent_fragments: 8
  max_top_k: 50
  max_chunks_per_file: 3
  fusion:
    enabled: false # enable only after offline golden-set evidence supports the candidate policy
    rrf_k: 60
    dense_weight: 1.0
    bm25_weight: 1.0
    exact_match_boost: 0.0
    header_match_boost: 0.0
    min_exact_tokens: 1
    min_header_tokens: 1
    profiles: {}

reranker:
  enabled: false   # opt in only after a measured gain on the current embedding profile
  addr: "http://localhost:5002"
  model: "BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3" # swappable sidecar cross-encoder (env RERANKER_MODEL overrides); revert to cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 for the tiny/fast baseline
  candidate_mul: 4     # fetch topK*4 candidates before reranking (more headroom for the reranker to reorder)
  request_timeout: 30s
  adaptive_enabled: false # opt in until release-gated judgments confirm no quality regression
  adaptive_margin_threshold: 0.01 # rerank when dense/lexical top results disagree or fused top margin is below 1%

# Local inference profile. LLM and embedding concurrency is owned by the
# Ollama scheduler (OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL) plus each role's request_timeout, so
# no client-side gate is imposed. The reranker keeps an explicit client-side
# queue; it is CPU by default for portable laptop operation — use the GPU
# Compose override with device=cuda only when Ollama and the reranker have a
# measured hardware budget.
inference:
  profile: "local"
  ollama:
    keep_alive: 5m
  reranker:
    max_concurrent: 1
    queue_timeout: 30s
    device: "cpu"
    backend: "torch"

# Process-local operation gates (bounded, finite queues). Indexing is
# single-writer; destructive mutations (document reset, chat edits and
# deletions) never run concurrently with an indexing pass. A request that
# waits longer than queue_timeout fails fast instead of piling up. LLM and
# embedding concurrency is NOT gated here — the Ollama scheduler owns it.
# These limits coordinate one API process only; they are not distributed.
gates:
  indexing:
    max_concurrent: 1
    queue_timeout: 5s
  destructive:
    max_concurrent: 1
    queue_timeout: 10s

enrichment:
  # Index-time LLM enrichment (uses Ollama; one-time cost per chunk, zero
  # query-time latency). Changing these requires a reindex to take effect.
  request_timeout: 120s
  contextual:
    enabled: false          # Anthropic-style LLM-written situational context prepended to each chunk before embedding
    ollama_addr: "http://localhost:11434"
    model: "gemma3:1b"

semantic_cache:
  enabled: true     # set true to enable; requires no extra infra (reuses Qdrant)
  collection: "p1_subject_cache_20261003"
  threshold: 0.90    # cosine similarity cutoff (0.85=permissive, 0.95=strict)
  ttl: 24h           # 0 = no expiry

generator:
  enabled: true      # set true + ensure the Ollama model is pulled; the dashboard or POST /api/v1/turns with generate=true
  ollama_addr: "http://localhost:11434"
  model: "gemma3:4b"  # LLM for answer generation; use instruct models. gemma3:4b passes the generation gate (ADR 0034: faithfulness 0.881 / relevancy 0.803 vs 1b 0.750/0.756) at ~9x answer latency; gemma3:1b is the low-latency fallback
  request_timeout: 120s
  max_output_tokens: 512 # bound answer generation; prevents an unending stream
  num_ctx: 4096          # pin the Ollama context window: prompt budget + instructions + output must fit (GENERATOR_NUM_CTX)

chat:
  # Chat use-case tuning: prompt assembly and the streaming turn lifecycle.
  max_context_tokens: 2800  # token budget for retrieved chunks (~70% of 4k ctx window)
  event_buffer: 4096
  max_event_log_bytes: 1048576   # 1 MiB replay log per turn
  max_retained_turns: 64
  finished_turn_ttl: 10m
  persist_timeout: 5s

rewriter:
  # Conversational query rewriting (Rewrite-Retrieve-Read): follow-up turns
  # are rewritten into standalone search queries against the session's last
  # `turns` turns before retrieval, so "what about the second one?" stops
  # searching garbage. Skipped when a session has no prior turns; any
  # rewrite failure falls back to the raw query. Costs +1 LLM call per
  # follow-up turn.
  enabled: true
  turns: 4           # prior turns fed to the rewriter
  request_timeout: 8s
  ollama_addr: "http://localhost:11434"
  model: "gemma3:1b"

history:
  enabled: true              # persists chat sessions/turns to Qdrant, no extra infra
  collection: "p1_subject_history_20261003"
  session_page_size: 50      # sidebar sessions returned per request
  turn_page_size: 500        # Qdrant scroll page used while loading one session

docling:
  enabled: false             # enable PDF intake when the Docling sidecar is available
  addr: "http://localhost:5003"
  request_timeout: 120s

turn.query: A worker finished after its Redis lock expired. Is it safe for it to delete the lock key now?

results.text: When the worker finishes, it should delete the marker only if the token still matches. Otherwise, a worker whose lock has expired could accidentally delete a newer worker's lock. The lock can also expire while work is still running, allowing another worker to start the same job. For important changes, make the operation safe to repeat or enforce uniqueness in the database that stores the result. A lock alone cannot prevent duplicate work after it expires

A Redis lock is a temporary marker that lets one worker claim a job. SET lock:resource <token> NX PX <milliseconds> creates the marker only if it does not exist (NX) and sets an expiry time (PX). Give each attempt a different token so Redis can tell which worker owns the marker.

Case C: Lock Deletion Safety (Lua Script) If Thread A's lock expires and Thread B acquires the key, Thread A's raw DEL could remove Thread B's lock. DISCO checks the trip ID in an atomic Lua script:
if redis.call("get", KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
    return redis.call("del", KEYS[1])
else
    return 0
end
ult. A lock alone cannot prevent duplicate work after it expires. The Redis distributed-lock guide explains the safety assumptions and failure cases.

Case B: Driver Declines or Times Out
If declined: DISCO deletes the lock with DEL driver:lock:drv_98765.
If timed out: Redis expires the key after 15 seconds. A background timer then tries Candidate #2.

How downstream consumers handle duplicates (Idempotency):
Using Primary Key / Idempotent Writes: In Elasticsearch or Redis, performing SET user:1 {name: 'Alexander'} 5 times yields the same result as doing it once.

results.text:
4. Handling "At-Least-Once" Delivery & Duplicate Data
Because committing the offset happens after sending the event to Kafka, a crash can occasionally lead to a scenario where LSN 580 was sent to Kafka, but the CDC engine crashed before updating its offset state to 580. When it recovers, it reads from LSN 410 again and re-sends LSN 580 to Kafka. This means CDC systems guarantee "At-Least-Once" event delivery, so downstream consumers (like your cache, search index, or microservices) must handle occasional duplicate events gracefully.

results.header: Structure of a CDC Event Payload
Choose when writes update the cache
results.text:
With a synchronous cache update, the application updates the database and cache as part of the request. Readers see the cache update sooner, but the two writes can disagree if one succeeds and the other fails. Redis and a separate database do not share an automatic transaction.
With an asynchronous update, the application queues work for a background worker to apply to the cache or source. This can shorten request handling, but readers may see old data until the worker catches up. The queue or event path must handle retries and duplicate messages, and the application must decide whether acknowledging the request before the update is durable is acceptable.
Cache-aside is another common choice: the application reads through Redis and fills the cache only after a miss. It avoids preloading the entire dataset, but requires a clear TTL and invalidation policy.

results.header: Why separate audio and video, and what is ABR packaging?
results.text:
Why separate audio and video? If bandwidth drops, the player can switch video quality while keeping one continuous audio track. A combined file would make that switch harder.
What is ABR packaging? It does not merge chunks into one video. It creates a manifest (.mpd for MPEG-DASH or .m3u8 for HLS) that indexes the encoded audio and video chunks. The manifest contains:
The web addresses (URLs) of every audio chunk.
The web addresses of every video chunk broken down by resolution and codec.
The exact timestamp alignment for every chunk.

When a creator uploads a video, YouTube processes it through an asynchronous Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) instead of one large conversion job:
Chunking: The upload service splits the video into 2–5 second GOP (Group of Pictures) chunks for parallel processing.
Transcoding DAG: Workers encode chunks into AV1, VP9, and H.264/AVC at multiple resolutions and frame rates.
Parallel workflows: Other DAG nodes create thumbnails, extract audio, generate captions, and scan audio against Content ID.
Adaptive bitrate (ABR) packaging: Encoded chunks are indexed in MPEG-DASH and HLS manifests (.mpd or .m3u8). The client selects quality based on network bandwidth and device performance.

Live streaming cannot use the standard VOD DAG because encoding must happen in real time:
Broadcaster
     │ RTMP/WebRTC
     v
Live ingress → Transcoder → LL-DASH → CDN → Viewer (1–3 s)
                   │
                   └─→ DVR store

Ingress protocols: Broadcasters push raw streams using RTMP, WebRTC, SRT, or DASH-PUT.
Low-Latency DASH (LL-DASH) and CMAF: Transcoders send sub-second chunks to the edge as they are generated.
DVR engine: Writes live segments to Colossus so viewers can rewind.

results.header: Ride-Matching System Design: Geospatial Search and Dispatch
results.text:
This conceptual ride-hailing design matches driver supply with rider demand using geospatial indexing, low-latency dispatch, and storage paths separated by access pattern.
It uses Uber's publicly discussed terminology as a reference point, but the diagrams and capacity choices below are an engineering model rather than an official description of Uber's current implementation.
The sections below cover the main parts.

results.header: How the AP vs. CP Trade-Off Shapes the System
results.text:
The platform uses different CAP trade-offs for different sub-domains:
| Engine | Requirement | Trade-off Choice | Storage Engine | Flow | |--------|-------------|----------------|----------------|------| | Location Tracking Engine | High Availability & Sub-second Latency | AP Eventual Consistency | Redis Spatial Cluster | → feeds into → | | Matching & Trip State Engine | Zero Double-Bookings, Financial Integrity | CP Strong Consistency | Distributed RDBMS (CockroachDB / Postgres) | |

Non-functional:
Low latency: Location ingestion < 50ms; matching decision < 1 second.
High throughput: Handle 1,000,000+ active drivers sending pings continuously.
Consistency: Assign each driver to at most one rider at a time.
High availability: 99.99% uptime without a single point of failure.

turn.query: Why must a worker compare its token before releasing a Redis lock?

results.text: A Redis lock is a temporary marker that lets one worker claim a job. SET lock:resource <token> NX PX <milliseconds> creates the marker only if it does not exist (NX) and sets an expiry time (PX). Give each attempt a different token so Redis can tell which worker owns the marker.

When the worker finishes, it should delete the marker only if the token still matches. Otherwise, a worker whose lock has expired could accidentally delete a newer worker's lock. The lock can also expire while work is still running, allowing another worker to start the same job. For important changes, make the operation safe to repeat or enforce uniqueness in the database that stores the result. A lock alone cannot prevent duplicate work after it expires

Phase 3: Lock and dispatch offer The selected driver has not accepted yet.
Acquire atomic lock: DISCO uses Redis (SETNX lock:driver_123 ride_999 EX 15) to reserve the top-ranked driver for 15 seconds.
Send the offer: If the lock succeeds, the notification service sends an offer to the Driver App.
Driver decision:If accepted: The lock becomes an active trip record in the primary database.
If declined or timed out: The lock expires and DISCO tries Candidate #2.

SETNX works on one Redis node. In a multi-region cluster, a primary could crash before replicating the lock.
Redlock: DISCO writes to five independent Redis masters. It grants a lock when at least three confirm SETNX within the timeout.

SET status = 'ON_TRIP', current_trip_id = 'ride_111'
WHERE driver_id = 'drv_98765' AND status = 'AVAILABLE';

results.header: When Do You Need Predefined Rules?
results.text:
You need predefined rules (or a predefined schema/ontology) for three critical tasks:
Schema Guardrails (Ontology): Define what node types (e.g., Person, Company, Event) and relationship predicates are legal. Without a strict ontology rule, an LLM might invent 50 different variations for the same action (bought, purchased, acquired_majority_stake_in), breaking graph queries.
Deterministic Data Normalization: Rules (like Regular Expressions) parse standardized data—timestamps (YYYY-MM-DD), monetary values ($2.6B → 2,600,000,000 USD), and legal IDs (tax numbers, stock tickers). Using an LLM for standard regex work wastes tokens and risks arithmetic errors.
Graph Integrity Checks: Logical rules prevent invalid connections (e.g., a rule stating a Person cannot be a SUBSIDIARY_OF another Person). If an extraction model proposes an invalid triple, rule-based validation drops it before it enters the database.

Structural/Ownership: SUBSIDIARY_OF, INVESTED_IN, EMPLOYED_BY

results.text:
Use the simplest option that protects the state transition. A script is not inherently faster for every operation: it can save round-trips when it replaces several client-server exchanges, but script execution also uses the Redis command thread.
Redis scripts provide atomic execution, not general rollback or a transaction with another service. For Redis 7 and later, Redis Functions are also available for server-side logic. See the official Lua scripting documentation and Redis Functions overview.

Lua lets an application send a short program to Redis. The script can read and update Redis data in one server-side execution. No other command runs between the script's Redis operations, so it can protect a check-and-update sequence without separate application round-trips.
Consider two riders trying to claim the same driver. A plain GET followed by SET can race. A Lua script can check the status and write the match in one execution:
-- KEYS[1]: driver:{123}:status
-- KEYS[2]: driver:{123}:match

The shared {123} hash tag keeps both keys in one Redis Cluster slot. The first script claims the driver; a later script sees that the status is no longer AVAILABLE. This protects the Redis update, not a later action in a separate database or service.

Case C: Lock Deletion Safety (Lua Script) If Thread A's lock expires and Thread B acquires the key, Thread A's raw DEL could remove Thread B's lock. DISCO checks the trip ID in an atomic Lua script:
if redis.call("get", KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
    return redis.call("del", KEYS[1])
else
    return 0
end
